title: Evaluating a Generate–Validate–Repair Pipeline for LLM‑based Network Configuration: a Paired, Emulation‑Grounded Study
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired, emulation‑grounded experiment (study id study-cand-1-gvr-verifier-adversarial-2026-08-01) to test whether integrating a deterministic network verifier into a generate–validate–repair (GVR) pipeline reduces the rate of unsafe configuration applications from an LLM relative to an LLM‑only pipeline. The experiment used declared model gpt-5-mini and a deterministic verifier (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) under shared_initial_candidate semantics (exactly one initial LLM generation per task, reused across arms); guarded episodes could request up to one validator‑triggered repair. N = 240 paired intent→configuration tasks were executed (144 in‑distribution, 48 distribution‑shift, 48 adversarial). All archived scoring artifacts report safe outcomes for every paired episode: baseline = 240/240 safe, guarded = 240/240 safe. The paired risk difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.00; 95% bootstrap percentile CI = [0.00, 0.00] (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729); exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. Under the preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics the guarded arm could only change outcomes by invoking a validator‑triggered repair; in this run every shared candidate passed deterministic validation and no repairs were applied. We report the preregistered design, artifact‑grounded execution accounting, the full analysis results, an evidence‑based explanation of the null paired outcome, and recommendations for future informative GVR evaluations.

sections.introduction: Translating high‑level operator intent into device configurations is critical to scalable NetOps. Recent work uses large language models (LLMs) to generate configuration change plans and full configurations, but token‑level correctness does not capture multi‑step ordering, dependency invariants, and transient states that determine whether a change is safe to apply. Closed‑loop, emulation‑grounded evaluation (where generated configurations are executed in device emulators and deterministically scored) exposes semantic failure modes—ordering mistakes, transient violations, protected‑resource touches—that text‑only tests miss. The generate–validate–repair (GVR) pattern pairs LLM generation with a deterministic verifier and automated repair; this pattern is widely proposed for reducing configuration failures but its empirical causal effect under distribution shift and adversarial prompts remains an open question. We designed and executed a preregistered, paired experiment to measure the absolute paired difference in unsafe_apply rate (guarded minus baseline) under carefully controlled semantics. The core contribution is an artifact‑grounded report of the preregistered estimand, the execution accounting, and an evidence‑based failure analysis explaining why the paired contrast in this run was degenerate.
sections.related_work: Executable NetOps benchmarks and emulation frameworks have recently been proposed to surface workflow and planning faults for LLM agents rather than only assessing textual fidelity; NetConfArena exemplifies this executable closed‑loop approach [1]. Generate–validate patterns appear in configuration‑repair and program‑repair literature and have yielded high repair coverage for many syntactic and local semantic faults, though effectiveness depends on verifier coverage and repair strategy [2], [4]. Surveys and position papers synthesize agentic architectures, tool augmentation, verifier integration, and uncertainty calibration as promising patterns for operational automation and safety [3], [5]. Engineering experience from configuration analysis tools (e.g., Batfish) informs verifier design and incremental verification strategies [6]. Our study differs: it combines (a) a preregistered paired estimand, (b) shared_initial_candidate execution semantics formalized in the preregistration, (c) emulation‑grounded deterministic scoring, and (d) full archival of execution and analysis artifacts to allow deterministic reconciliation between the estimand and reported outputs.
sections.methodology: Preregistration and estimand: We preregistered the study and estimand prior to execution. The primary estimand is the absolute paired difference in unsafe_apply rate (guarded minus baseline) where each task yields a binary final outcome: unsafe_apply (1) if the final configuration would cause a semantic safety violation when applied in the emulator, and safe_apply (0) otherwise. Design and sampling: The design is paired with shared_initial_candidate semantics: exactly one initial LLM generation is produced per task and reused by both arms; the guarded arm may request up to one validator‑triggered repair. We executed N = 240 paired tasks blocked into topology/vendor clusters and composed as 60% in‑distribution (144), 20% distribution‑shift (48), and 20% adversarial (48). Model and adapter contract: Execution declared model gpt-5-mini and used an adapter pattern that enforces the shared_initial_candidate contract; the deterministic verifier used is deterministic_netops_validator_v5. Scoring and exclusions: A deterministic emulator+validator pipeline assigns a binary final outcome. Predeclared exclusions included pairs flagged as potential verifier false‑safe (validator PASS but emulator unsafe outcome) and unrecoverable infrastructure failures; these were to be treated per the preregistered missingness plan. Statistical analysis: Primary analysis used a paired binary estimator, exact McNemar test on discordant pairs, and bootstrap percentile 95% CIs with 10,000 resamples (bootstrap_seed = 1729). Secondary planned analyses included repair counts and model‑call budgets per task.
sections.results: Execution accounting: The run completed according to the preregistered plan. Exactly one initial generation per task was produced and consumed; model calls used = 240 and planned episodes = 480 were completed (complete pairs = 240). Missingness and exclusions: No infra failures or predeclared exclusions occurred; all pairs were scorable. Primary outcomes: Every paired episode was scored safe under both arms: baseline successes = 240/240, guarded successes = 240/240. The paired contingency is n11 = 240 (both safe), n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. Estimated paired risk difference (guarded_unsafe_rate − baseline_unsafe_rate) = 0.00. Bootstrap percentile 95% CI = [0.00, 0.00] (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729). Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. Validator and repair activity: No validator‑triggered repairs were applied (repair_invocations = 0 across the run); every shared initial candidate passed deterministic validation. Subgroup slices (in‑distribution, shift, adversarial) are degenerate (all zeros) given the global outcome.
sections.discussion: Mechanistic explanation for the null paired contrast: Under the preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics, the single shared generation per task is reused by both arms; the guarded arm can only create discordant outcomes by having that shared candidate fail validation and then applying a validator‑triggered repair. In this execution every shared candidate passed deterministic verification and repairs were never invoked; therefore the guarded arm could not produce discordant pairs and the paired contrast is necessarily degenerate. Design tradeoffs: shared_initial_candidate semantics reduce model‑call budget and guarantee a directly paired generator sample, but they also make the detectability of verifier benefit contingent on initial candidate failures. To causally measure verifier effectiveness one must provide opportunities for the verifier to act (for example by allowing independent initial generations per arm, increasing adversary strength, or expanding the repair budget). Threats to validity: internal validity is constrained by the shared‑candidate contract; construct validity depends on verifier semantic coverage; external validity is limited by the emulation corpus and single model tested; conclusion validity is limited when realized baseline failure rates are zero and produce uninformative discordant counts.
sections.conclusion: We conducted a preregistered, paired, emulation‑grounded evaluation of a GVR pipeline for LLM‑based network configuration. Observed outcome: every paired episode was safe under both arms, yielding a paired difference of 0.00 (95% bootstrap CI [0.00, 0.00]; McNemar p = 1.0). The preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics and the deterministic verifier behavior explain the null paired contrast: because a single shared candidate per task was produced and that candidate passed verification every time, the guarded arm had no opportunity to apply repairs and therefore could not differ from baseline. We present artifact‑grounded execution accounting, reconciled statistical outputs, and concrete recommendations for future experimental designs that can produce informative paired contrasts by altering generation semantics, adversary strength, or repair allowance. These recommendations and our reconciled artifacts aim to guide reproducible, informative evaluations of verifier‑assisted LLM NetOps pipelines.

disclosure_statement: Execution used declared model gpt-5-mini under the hosted_netops_gvr_v1 adapter; the guarded pipeline employed deterministic_netops_validator_v5 and permitted up to one validator‑triggered repair per task. The study was preregistered (study id study-cand-1-gvr-verifier-adversarial-2026-08-01) and executed under the frozen plan after the autonomy lock; the human Research Director selected the topic family and constrained the initial master prompt before the lock. The adapter used shared_initial_candidate semantics (one shared initial generation per task reused across both arms), so paired divergences could only arise if the shared candidate failed deterministic validation or if a validator‑triggered repair was applied. The immutable initial master prompt is archived at provenance/master_prompt.txt (SHA‑256: 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba). Execution artifacts (preregistration, execution manifest, per‑call traces, validator traces, and analysis artifacts) are archived with the study bundle for reproducibility. No manual human editing of the technical manuscript content occurred after the autonomy lock.
limitations: Emulator and corpus scope: tasks used a synthetic emulation corpus; external validity to production multi‑vendor deployments and operator workflows is limited.
Single model: a single hosted model (gpt-5-mini) was tested; results do not imply generality across other models, prompt formulations, or prompting strategies.

Shared_initial_candidate semantics: the paired design produced one shared initial generation per task; this prevents generator variability between arms and makes verifier benefit contingent on initial candidate failures.
Adversary bounds: adversarial prompts were generated under a preregistered, fixed adversary protocol and do not represent unconstrained or adaptive adversaries.
Verifier coverage: the deterministic verifier encodes a finite set of semantic checks; undetected semantic fault classes could remain and would affect practical safety outcomes.
